sections.name: 二、檐很多，出檐深远
sections.content_zh:
二、檐很多，出檐深远

温州乡土住宅从造型角度讲，它的最大特色表现在檐上：屋面外伸形成很深的屋檐（照2-1）；檐的门类很多，出檐很深，一般占檐柱高的一半（照2-2）；在楼房分层处设腰檐（照2-3）；局部屋面升高，形成重檐（照2-4）；为保护山面不遭雨淋，产生山檐（照2-5）；室外走廊多以披屋形式处理，又产生廊檐（照2-11）；在山面或没有腰檐的墙面上开窗、开门加上雨坡，成为窗檐、门檐（照2-10）；有些食物、种子需藏在通风、防湿的地方，故又创造了檐箱（照2-7，照2-8，照2-9）；为适应沿海风大的特点，在主体建筑山墙的两端往往加坡，以抵住主体的山墙，增加了建筑物的刚度，同时披屋面遮住了主体建筑山墙的大部分，折过来，又减少太阳的辐射，这种披屋，可看作是扩大了的檐（照2-16）。百褶裙似的居屋，如一株阔叶树，枝叶扶疏，春意盎然（照2-5）。同时，屋与屋相连形成连绵之景。

檐还有生产意义上的作用，廊檐下是堆放杂物、晾衣、纺纱、置磨、搁风车的好地方；檐相当于今天的窗台，是置放蚕床、晒鞋、晒食物等的场所（照2-4，照2-14）。各式各样的檐箱，使人想起鸟巢，依附在几片树叶下，构筑起一个小家，成为农家贮藏食物种子等小件物品的地方，同时还有美化居室的作用（照2-13）。

这些檐又派生出另一个特色，即造就了丰富的山墙和生动的屋角（照2-15）。很多住宅的屋角头，因此成为家庭活动的重心（照2-16，照2-18）。有些住宅两层楼房的腰檐与山檐相交，在山墙上挑出一片斜面，或者，在转角上断开，形成一个小巧的山尖（照2-17）。有的山尖做得很大，具有"亭"的作用（照2-23）。有些住宅山墙面上用一排细长的斜撑，支承披檐，增加了山墙前空间的层次和形式变化，把力的传递表现得轻松自如。更有甚者，有些住宅把楼梯做在山墙山尖下，体现了山民的野性（照2-19）。这儿的山墙，大部分是木板或竹帘糊上草泥做的，木板一般为原色，草泥糊的山墙一般刷上一道石灰，也有刷砺灰（贝壳碾碎烧制而成）的。深深挑出的檐和桁条，白色（灰色）透薄的墙面，凹凸的梁柱，产生玲珑的结构感（照2-6）。

温州乡土民居中也有用砖砌的封护山墙，这些山墙往往做成观音兜式或五花、弓背，山墙的轮廓线很有弹性、很有生气（照14-3）。

一字形屋有两个山墙，H形屋有四个山墙，温州古代的匠师们不满足在这些山墙上做文章，就连"门"形住宅，后面的两个角也都向后和向外侧做出山墙来。后面两个山墙是厢房的，侧面的两个山墙是正房的。

深入温州农村，人们会得到一个印象，温州乡土建筑最丰富的地方是檐，最富机巧、最有生气的地方是屋角和山墙，它往往代替了现代观念中的正立面而成为主立面（照2-15）。我国古代正统建筑的主要精力放在第五立面（屋顶）上，温州乡土民居则放在头顶的稍下一点——檐上，这是有其深刻原因的。

檐字在古代《说文解字》中："檐、棍也"，棍，即连绵之状。古代"棍"、"槾"通用，"槾"为"楣"之意。中国的古文字是社会的写照，也是实践活动的结果，檐字点出了温州乡土建筑的基本特征，勾画出温州的气候、地形地貌和社会经济、生产面貌的基本特点。历史上，王羲之和谢灵运都任过温州太守，他们的人格、字韵、诗品都可以说受过温州山水的孕育，反之，也可以引证温州山水和建筑。温州溪边浣衣女的"鹅兜"参差成群，仿佛由王右军饲养的白鹅变成，谢灵运诗如"芙蓉出水"，温州乡土民居众檐确具有鹅兜参差、芙蓉出水之美。
sections.content_en:
2. Many Eaves, Deep Overhangs

From a造型 perspective, the greatest feature of Wenzhou vernacular residences is expressed in the eaves: the roof extends outward to form very deep eaves (photo 2-1); there are many types of eaves, with deep overhangs, generally half the height of the eave column (photo 2-2); waist eaves are set at floor divisions of multi-story buildings (photo 2-3); local roof surfaces are raised to form double eaves (photo 2-4); to protect gable ends from rain, gable eaves are created (photo 2-5); outdoor corridors are mostly treated as lean-to structures, creating corridor eaves (photo 2-11); windows and doors on gable ends or walls without waist eaves are given rain slopes, becoming window eaves and door eaves (photo 2-10); some food and seeds need to be stored in ventilated, moisture-proof places, so eave boxes were created (photos 2-7, 2-8, 2-9); to adapt to the strong coastal winds, slopes are often added at both ends of the main building's gable walls to resist the main gable walls, increasing the building's rigidity; at the same time, the lean-to roof covers most of the main building's gable wall, folding over to reduce solar radiation. This lean-to can be seen as an enlarged eave (photo 2-16). Residences like pleated skirts, like a broad-leaf tree with lush branches and leaves, full of spring vitality (photo 2-5). At the same time, houses connected to each other form a continuous scene.

Eaves also have productive significance: under corridor eaves are good places for stacking杂物, drying clothes, spinning, placing mills and winnowing machines; eaves are equivalent to today's window sills, places for placing silkworm beds, drying shoes, drying food, etc. (photos 2-4, 2-14). Various eave boxes remind people of bird nests, attached under a few leaves, building a small home, becoming places for farmers to store small items such as food and seeds, while also beautifying the residence (photo 2-13).

These eaves also give rise to another feature, namely creating rich gable walls and vivid roof corners (photo 2-15). Many houses' roof corners thus become the center of family activities (photos 2-16, 2-18). Some two-story houses' waist eaves intersect with gable eaves, projecting a sloped surface on the gable wall, or breaking at the corner to form a small gable tip (photo 2-17). Some gable tips are made very large, functioning as a "pavilion" (photo 2-23). Some residences use a row of slender diagonal braces on the gable wall to support the lean-to eave, increasing the layers and formal variations of the space in front of the gable wall, expressing force transmission with ease. What's more, some houses put stairs under the gable tip, reflecting the wildness of mountain dwellers (photo 2-19). The gable walls here are mostly made of wooden boards or bamboo curtains pasted with grass-mud; wooden boards are generally in natural color, grass-mud gable walls are generally painted with a layer of lime, and some are painted with oyster ash (made from crushed and fired shells). The deeply projecting eaves and purlins, white (gray) translucent walls, and凹凸 beams and columns create an exquisite structural sense (photo 2-6).

Wenzhou vernacular residences also have brick-sealed gable walls, often made in Guanyin-bao style or five-flower, bow-back styles, with elastic and vivid gable wall outlines (photo 14-3).

A one-line house has two gable walls, an H-shaped house has four gable walls. Ancient Wenzhou craftsmen were not satisfied with working only on these gable walls; even in "门"-shaped (U-shaped) houses, the rear two corners also have gable walls made backward and outward. The rear two gable walls belong to the wing rooms, and the side two gable walls belong to the main house.

Going deep into Wenzhou's countryside, one gets the impression that the richest part of Wenzhou vernacular architecture is the eaves, and the most ingenious and lively parts are the roof corners and gable walls, which often replace the modern concept of the front facade to become the main facade (photo 2-15). The main energy of ancient Chinese orthodox architecture was placed on the fifth facade (roof), while Wenzhou vernacular residences placed it slightly below the top — the eaves, which has profound reasons.

The character "檐" (eave) in the ancient "Shuowen Jiezi" (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters): "Eave, gun also"; gun means continuous state. In ancient times, "gun" and "man" were interchangeable, and "man" means "lintel." Chinese ancient characters are reflections of society and results of practical activities; the character for eave points out the basic characteristics of Wenzhou vernacular architecture, delineating the basic features of Wenzhou's climate, topography, and socio-economic and productive aspects. Historically, both Wang Xizhi and Xie Lingyun served as prefects of Wenzhou; their personalities, calligraphy, and poetry can be said to have been nurtured by Wenzhou's landscapes, and conversely, they also testify to Wenzhou's landscapes and architecture. The "geese baskets" of laundry women by Wenzhou's streams are clustered in irregular groups, as if transformed from the white geese raised by Wang Xizhi (Wang Youjun); Xie Lingyun's poetry is like "lotus emerging from water," and the numerous eaves of Wenzhou vernacular residences indeed possess the beauty of irregular geese baskets and lotus emerging from water.

key_terms.en: Many eaves, deep overhangs (Wenzhou residence feature)

sections.name: 三、横向发展，开敞通透
sections.content_zh:
三、横向发展，开敞通透

温州乡土建筑的第三个地方特色是开敞、通透。中国古建筑以群体之美为特征，温州乡土民居大多数是独立的，房屋外向开敞，四个面都开门开窗，不设防、不拒人，它没有江南一带官宦府弟的跋扈气势和奢靡装饰，既不同于粉墙包裹着雕梁画栋、颇有书卷气、带有内省气质的徽商住宅，也不像北方的四合院和江浙一带的天井式及云南的一颗印式民居，把自己围合得很严密；温州民居独立对外（照3-1），一方面纳四方之风景尽入户中，另方面突出于环境之中，成为人们欣赏的对象。它是心平气和的，无须为了安全和财富将自己包装起来，普通老百姓的房屋不用砖墙体，完全展示通身的木构架，木肌里，表达质朴的美（照3-2，照3-3）；而它又是谦逊温和的，不必雕镂藻饰、厅堂轩昂地显示富有和权势，它只在檐下辟一廊，人们休闲其中，流露出山野平民的生活气息（照3-4）。其房屋平面布局以一字形和三合院门居多，打破了"人之宅不过三间五架"的等级制度。普通人的住宅，不像在面宽的限制下只能向纵深发展的官宦大屋，它可自由地横向发展。横向发展成为它的一大特征（照3-5），面宽超过五开间的比比皆是，至于七、九、十一开间的长屋也屡见不鲜，甚至出现了十五开间的长屋（照14-5）。还有一种三合院的变种H型，也呈开敞性质。一字形房屋小巧而富于变化，加上旁侧的厕所、储屋、猪栏等，造成体型和层次的穿插，使整个村子都显得开敞、明朗，体形活泼。"门"形的民居比较模式化，院前多不设墙，即使有，院墙的高度亦低于厢房底层披檐，院内的树木、瓜果都越墙透出（照6-8）。更富特点的是正屋和两厢的山墙面和背面大部分作木板壁，在板壁上开门、开窗用直棂窗，堂屋前檐完全敞开，没有装修。家家楼房一般都不做楼梯，而用竹梯，上下的位置也不固定，更加显示出自然的开敞的特色。村落中长条形房子居多，形成了整个村子开敞通透、明朗活泼的格局。

民居平面为田、目等形状时，可使建筑呈封闭型，隐现"内聚"和"藏"的底蕴，但就居住房间本身来说仍是开敞的：办法之一是做大天井，即在屋内设院（照8-6）。浙中、浙西的天井式四合院和这儿相比，其天井是很小的，天井内不能种树植花；而温州的院落，可种树种花，有生产空间意义，天井不但大而且数量多。如永嘉芙蓉村大屋、平阳顺溪陈宅、泰顺雪溪胡宅都布置了前后院落，围合了很多天井，使房间都处于自然气息（院和天井）的氛围中；办法之二是布置大尺度的"堂屋"和檐廊。堂屋，温州人叫作"上间"，面宽一般4～5m，有的达6m以上。浙中、浙西的天井式住宅，堂屋前檐没有装修，空间与天井直接相融；温州大户民居从房间到院用廊过渡，连两厢也设檐廊（照14-2）。檐廊是日常生活的主要场所（照2-11），夏天纳凉，冬天负暄，老人晒太阳，小孩嬉游，汉子打牌，妇女纺织，都在这些廊下。

温州乡土民居除檐、廊外，还有一个特殊的做法是明间檐柱之间没有枋子联系，形成了一个空档，这也使房子产生开敞通透的效果。《鲁班经》里曾说，人站在堂屋的太师壁前向外望时，应该看到门口的上槛背后衬着天空，不应该看到柱子间的枋子、檐口或其他东西。

综上所述，温州乡下的大户人家的屋房，运用众多的宽敞的天井（院落）、胸墙、檐廊，明间柱间不设额枋，以及四面开窗、开门等各种方法，加上精湛的小木作技巧，解决了大屋的通风、采光等问题，取得了开敞通透的效果。
sections.content_en:
3. Horizontal Development, Open and Transparent

The third local characteristic of Wenzhou vernacular architecture is openness and transparency. Ancient Chinese architecture is characterized by the beauty of groups; most Wenzhou vernacular residences are independent, with houses open to the outside, doors and windows on all four sides, undefended and welcoming. They lack the overbearing aura and extravagant decoration of official mansions in the Jiangnan region; they are different from Huizhou merchant residences wrapped in whitewashed walls with carved beams and painted rafters, scholarly and introspective; they are also unlike northern quadrangles or Jiangzhe courtyard-style and Yunnan "one-seal" residences that enclose themselves tightly. Wenzhou residences are independently outward-facing (photo 3-1): on the one hand, they bring scenery from all directions into the home; on the other hand, they stand out in the environment as objects of appreciation. They are calm and gentle, with no need to wrap themselves up for safety and wealth; ordinary people's houses do not use brick walls, fully displaying their wooden frames and wood grain, expressing rustic beauty (photos 3-2, 3-3); and they are humble and mild, without need for carved ornamentation or grand halls to display wealth and power. They only set a corridor under the eaves where people relax, revealing the life atmosphere of mountain commoners (photo 3-4). Their house plane layouts are mostly one-line and three-sided courtyard types, breaking the hierarchical system that "a commoner's house should not exceed three bays and five frames." Ordinary people's residences, unlike official mansions that can only develop in depth due to width restrictions, can freely develop horizontally. Horizontal development has become a major feature (photo 3-5); residences with more than five bays are everywhere, and long houses of seven, nine, or even eleven bays are common, with even fifteen-bay long houses appearing (photo 14-5). There is also a variant of the three-sided courtyard, the H-type, which is also open in nature. One-line houses are small and varied, and with side toilets, storage rooms, pigsties, etc., creating interlocking volumes and layers, making the entire village appear open, bright, and lively in form. "门"-shaped (U-shaped) residences are more formulaic, often without walls in front of the courtyard; even if there are walls, the wall height is lower than the lean-to eaves of the wing room ground floor, allowing trees and fruits in the courtyard to peek over the wall (photo 6-8). A more distinctive feature is that the gable ends and backs of the main house and two wings are mostly wooden board walls, with doors and windows using straight-bar lattice windows on the board walls; the front eaves of the main hall are completely open, without finishing. Every household's buildings generally do not have built-in stairs, using bamboo ladders instead, with unfixed positions for going up and down, further showing the natural open characteristic. Long条形 houses are predominant in villages, forming an open, transparent, bright, and lively pattern throughout the village.

When the residence plane is in tian (field) or mu (eye) shapes, the building can be enclosed, showing the connotation of "inward gathering" and "concealment," but the living rooms themselves are still open: one method is to make large courtyards, i.e., setting yards within the house (photo 8-6). Compared with courtyard quadrangles in central and western Zhejiang, their courtyards are very small and cannot be planted with trees and flowers; while Wenzhou's courtyards can be planted with trees and flowers, having productive spatial significance, with courtyards not only large but also numerous. For example, the large house in Furong Village, Yongjia, the Chen residence in Shunxi, Pingyang, and the Hu residence in Xuexi, Taishun all have front and rear courtyards, enclosing many courtyards, placing all rooms in an atmosphere of natural气息 (courtyards and patios); the second method is to arrange large-scale "main halls" and eaves corridors. The main hall, called "shangjian" by Wenzhou people, generally has a width of 4-5m, some reaching over 6m. In courtyard-style residences in central and western Zhejiang, the front eaves of the main hall have no finishing, with space directly merging with the courtyard; in large Wenzhou residences, the transition from rooms to courtyards uses corridors, with even the two wings having eaves corridors (photo 14-2). Eaves corridors are the main places for daily life (photo 2-11): enjoying cool in summer, basking in sun in winter, elderly people sunbathing, children playing, men playing cards, women weaving — all happen under these corridors.

Besides eaves and corridors, Wenzhou vernacular residences have a special practice: there is no beam connecting the eave columns of the central bay, forming a gap, which also creates an open and transparent effect for the house. The "Lu Ban Jing" (Lu Ban Classic) once said that when a person stands in front of the taishi wall (master wall) of the main hall looking outward, they should see the sky behind the upper threshold of the doorway, and should not see beams between columns, eaves, or other things.

In summary, the large houses in Wenzhou's countryside use numerous spacious courtyards, chest walls, eaves corridors, no header beams between central bay columns, and various methods of opening windows and doors on all sides, coupled with exquisite small-woodwork techniques, to solve the ventilation and lighting problems of large houses, achieving an open and transparent effect.

sections.name: 四、木构架——深厚的历史渊源，精湛的薪传技艺
sections.content_zh:
四、木构架——深厚的历史渊源，精湛的薪传技艺

温州乡土建筑的第四个地方特色是木构架上具有深厚的历史渊源和精湛的薪传技艺，从整栋房子的大木结构到细部的小木装修，运用木材的技巧为其他地方所少见。更为惊叹的是保留了大量古老的木作技法，可称得上是古建筑的宝库，建筑形态以宋风为主要特征。

1. 梁架、斗栱、铺作

温州大户人家的建筑都用抬梁式，一般民居两端山墙面都用穿斗式。山区穿斗式木构架山面的上部，普遍用竹篱糊上砺灰筑成，既减轻了梁柱负荷，又取得了灵巧的结构感。其屋顶多为悬山顶，挑檐很深，木桁条直接架于梁上；一般为小木做，梁、坊与柱采用榫卯连接，用料粗犷硕大。正是这些纹路清晰、质地细韧、质感强烈的材料，得以使早年的木匠们在建筑裁剪时一气呵成，创造出无数浑然佳构，显示出山野人的豁达性格（照4-1）。山区一般民居多为小木屋，临街（路）木屋层层外挑，当地人有"占天不占地"之说（照2-13）。

温州乡土民居结构上第一个特点是，正屋檐柱连线与厢房檐柱连线相交的阴角不设落地柱，而设一个垂花柱（亦叫垂莲柱、花兰柱、冬瓜柱）（照4-1，照4-4），其做法是把厢房的檐枋架在正屋的枋子上，相交处倒挂下这个柱头。这个柱头不仅有传递力的作用，也是匠师们大显身手的地方——被刻成各种类型、十分精致的圆柱；第二个特点是每两柱之间置月梁，梁上立支承柱（照4-3，照4-8）；第三个特点是正屋先建，厢房待建，为了在两端结束正屋的挑檐檩，则从垂花柱上按45°斜角突出一段短短的挑梁，把挑檐端点架住。

温州乡土建筑中大木作的一些重要特点基本和宋式建筑相同，尤其是温州的祠堂更接近宋代的《营造法式》，它不仅每柱上都有栌斗，而且在于起结构作用的月梁，不是插入柱身，而是架于栌斗上（照4-8），明乳栿虽一端插入柱身，但另一端必置于檐柱栌斗内，而江南一带的厅堂普遍不是这样做法。另外，民居、祠堂中有柱与屋脊的升起及柱的侧脚等，这些做法，在明清时代的宫式建筑中已极为罕见。

温州乡土建筑中保留了大量宋风，不仅仅在于梁架结构方式上，其下考究的铺作是更为明显的说明。从整体来看，温州民居的檐下做法各式各样，异彩纷呈，以不同的区域、不同建造年代而各异，从整体上讲，铺作及檐下构件较质朴，颇具宋风；民居中，一般只在檐柱、前步柱及二层檐柱上坐栌斗、施铺作，虽然历代帝王都严禁庶民宅施重藻井，到明代甚至严禁任何斗栱的使用。但这里乡土建筑中斗栱使用仍十分普遍，宗祠庙宇、戏台、亭阁上的斗栱做得比较华丽，民居中的斗栱从功能上、视觉上都趋向于实用、简洁、少有夸张。很有意思的是，一些有身份的人，住宅门上几乎都做了砖的斗栱，起了极好的装饰作用。住宅一般只在柱头上安一个坐斗，形式古老，多为圆的或圆角海棠瓣的，很少用方形的坐斗；只有在檐廊里穿插枋和抱头梁上承接卷棚或井口轩的枋子或檩子的小构架上，有方形的坐斗。有些住宅的柱头上做出一个翘托住挑檐檩，少数讲究的有正心瓜栱和厢栱。

温州永嘉一带的斗栱做法较多古制，柱头有明显卷杀，柱顶坐栌斗，檐柱上多用圆栌斗，这种栌斗宋时出现，后来发展出各类瓜棱形斗、海棠形斗，在东阳等地的民居中多见。而这种质朴的圆栌斗似乎仅于温州一带能见，栌斗上缠有一匝当地人称为"白藤"的藤条，十分结实，用来防止栌斗开裂。额上及月梁上的坐斗一般斗欹较高，占斗高的5/9，而宋代斗欹仅占斗高的2/5，由于它特殊的比例（姑且称为"高脚斗"），产生的作用近于蜀柱用以抬高枋。

一般檐柱上有简单的一跳斗栱，《营造法式》中称为"斗口跳"（图11-5）；即栌斗横出泥道拱承托柱头枋及檐，纵向外出华栱一跳，跳头上施令栱，替木承撩檐，向内减拱承月梁，月梁有时与令栱上的耍头连做与横的各枋相交加固，耍头作麻叶云。清末民初的一些民居受江南建筑影响较大，干脆省去斗栱，并将轩梁挑出，做一道华板，板上承枋传。

还有一种斜撑栱，一头插入柱身，或立于丁头栱上，另一头置斗承枋（照4-9）。这种斜撑拱其实与徽州盛行的斜撑同源。徽州及东阳的这类斜撑成为装饰的重点，明代还多见流云卷草的较朴素纹样，至清朝就出现了繁冗的圆雕。温州这类斜撑拱与福建永安、太宁地区的这类构件极相似，上端持斗，下端作曲水纹，雕刻精美。另外，在泰顺、平阳一带可见类似关刀栱的插栱构件，有的斗栱退化为花冠形（图11-3），这一类斗栱与福建龙岩等地的做法相类似。以上两种斗栱做法都表明温州民居与福建民居在木作上的相互影响。

3. 屋面

温州乡土建筑整体上看起来十分生动飘逸，这种韵味的产生，一方面要归功于各种檐，另一方面是屋顶的处理，运用了举折、生起和侧脚的手法。屋面上下弯曲叫举折，左右弯曲叫生起，侧脚就是柱子向中心倾斜。

温州的气候闷热，房屋需要避免阳光直射，又需要挡风，因此，进深很大，出檐深，这样，屋面也就很大。屋面大了，就会呆板单调，由于用了举折、生起、侧脚三种做法，使房屋产生了两个曲面。从山墙看房子，由于举折做法，产生了一个微微弯曲的"人"字（图9-3）；从高处看屋脊，由于生起的做法，产生了一条扁担一样向两头微翘起的曲线（照1-5，照5-11），使屋面生动而有灵气，并且充满张力。整个村子虽然到处是屋顶，不但不沉闷，反而有一种亲和、轻快的气息。

这里的建筑，就连一些单坡，甚至连门屋、厕所之类的顶也要作举折和生起处理。它的主要做法是靠"升头木"或者垫瓦等。温州乡土建筑中凡小型的、形象完整表现出来的如亭子、寨门、牌楼、院门，侧脚是必有的，这种做法，一是加强了形象的整体感，二是使结构更加稳定，三是反衬出屋顶的舒展飘逸。

4. 小木作

民居中前廊后多安隔扇门，扇心一般为较朴素的棂花（参照4-16，照4-18），多为直条交拼如宫式、书条式，少用曲纹，不同于徽州、苏南一带棂花的繁芜，明式柳条窗也颇多，至于檐则多安装直棂窗。总之，温州山区村民崇尚朴素自然，不喜靡费，所以，整个装修上也少饰浮华，更具质朴的书卷气（照4-17，照4-20）。

温州民居的木作体系，不如官式木作规范化、纯正化，而更多地呈现出多元化，即受到不同地区、时代的影响，相互融和，取长补短，当然也不失本地区特色。例如，温州地区，虽然受到苏、皖、闽以及本省民居木作的影响，但仍保存了它自己可贵的木作传统，即一脉相承的宋代遗风与朴素自然、爱好天然曲材的风尚。所以，在民居木作的研究中，不仅要理清它本身木作的诸特征，还要纵横向加以联系，一方面探寻木作在历史上的演进，另一方面考察各地民间木作的相互影响。另外一条重要的线索，是官式建筑与民间建筑的相互联系。这两者之间并非"井水不犯河水"，而是相互交流、相互借鉴补充。这就如同舞蹈、戏曲等文化艺术，民间的文化是官方艺术或高雅艺术的源泉、基础，为其提供养料，而官方艺术又反过来影响民间的创作。
sections.content_en:
4. Timber Frame — Deep Historical Origins, Exquisite Hereditary Craftsmanship

The fourth local characteristic of Wenzhou vernacular architecture is that its timber frame has deep historical origins and exquisite hereditary craftsmanship. From the large timber structure of the entire house to the detailed small wood finishing, the skill in using wood is rarely seen elsewhere. What is even more amazing is that it preserves a large number of ancient woodworking techniques, truly a treasure trove of ancient architecture, with architectural forms mainly characterized by Song dynasty style.

1. Beam Frame, Dougong Bracket Sets, and Bracket Systems

Large houses in Wenzhou all use post-and-lintel (tailiang) construction, while the gable ends of ordinary residences generally use column-and-tie (chuandou) construction. In the upper part of the gable surface of mountain-area column-and-tie timber frames, bamboo fences pasted with oyster ash are commonly used, which both reduces the load on beams and columns and achieves a灵巧 structural sense. Their roofs are mostly overhanging gable (xuanshan) roofs with deep overhanging eaves, and wooden purlins are directly placed on beams; generally small wood construction, with beams, tie beams and columns connected by mortise and tenon joints, using rough and large materials. It is precisely these materials with clear grain, fine and tough texture, and strong quality that allowed early carpenters to complete architectural cutting in one go, creating countless natural and excellent structures, showing the open-minded character of mountain people (photo 4-1). Mountain-area ordinary residences are mostly small wooden houses, with street-facing wooden houses overhanging layer by layer; locals say they "occupy sky but not land" (photo 2-13).

The first structural feature of Wenzhou vernacular residences is that at the internal corner where the eave column line of the main house intersects with the eave column line of the wing room, no ground column is set, but a hanging lotus column (also called chuilian column, hualan column, donggua column) is installed (photos 4-1, 4-4). The practice is to place the eave tie beam of the wing room on the tie beam of the main house, with this column head hanging down at the intersection. This column head not only has the function of transmitting force, but is also a place where master craftsmen show their skills — carved into various types of very exquisite cylindrical columns. The second feature is that a moon beam (yueliang) is placed between every two columns, with support columns on the beam (photos 4-3, 4-8). The third feature is that the main house is built first, with the wing rooms to be built later; to end the overhanging eave purlins at both ends of the main house, a short cantilever beam protrudes at a 45° angle from the hanging lotus column to support the end of the overhanging eave.

Some important features of large timber construction in Wenzhou vernacular architecture are basically the same as Song-style architecture; especially Wenzhou ancestral halls are closer to the Song dynasty "Yingzao Fashi" (State Building Standards). Not only does every column have a ludou (cap block), but the structurally functional moon beam is not inserted into the column body but rests on the ludou (photo 4-8). Although one end of the mingrufu (exposed beam) is inserted into the column body, the other end must be placed in the ludou of the eave column, which is generally not the practice in halls of the Jiangnan region. Additionally, residences and ancestral halls have column and ridge rise (shengqi) and column inclination (cejiao), practices that have become extremely rare in Ming and Qing dynasty official-style architecture.

Wenzhou vernacular architecture preserves a great deal of Song style, not only in beam frame structural methods, but its elaborate bracket systems (puzuo) are even more obvious evidence. Overall, the practices under the eaves of Wenzhou residences are varied and colorful, differing by region and construction era. Generally speaking, the bracket systems and components under the eaves are relatively simple, with strong Song style. In residences, ludou and puzuo are generally only placed on eave columns, front step columns, and second-floor eave columns. Although successive emperors strictly prohibited commoners' residences from using elaborate coffered ceilings, and by the Ming dynasty even prohibited any use of dougong bracket sets, here dougong are still very commonly used in vernacular architecture. Dougong on ancestral halls, temples, stages, and pavilions are more ornate, while dougong in residences tend to be practical, simple, and rarely exaggerated in function and visual effect. Interestingly, some people of status have brick dougong on their residence doors, serving an excellent decorative function. Residences generally only place a zuodou (seat block) on column heads, in ancient forms, mostly round or round-cornered begonia-petal shaped, rarely using square seat blocks; only on the small frames supporting the purlins or tie beams of rolled-roof or well-ceilinged corridors under the eave corridor's chuancha fang and baotou beam are there square seat blocks. Some residences have a qiao (arm) on the column head supporting the overhanging eave purlin; a few elaborate ones have zhengxin guagong and xianggong.

In the Yongjia area of Wenzhou, dougong practices are more ancient, with column heads having obvious roll-cut (juansha) ends, ludou on column tops, and mostly round ludou on eave columns. This type of ludou appeared in the Song dynasty, later developing into various melon-ribbed and begonia-shaped dou, commonly seen in residences in Dongyang and other places. This simple round ludou seems to be found only in the Wenzhou area; the ludou is wrapped with a匝 of rattan called "baiteng" by locals, very strong, used to prevent the ludou from cracking. The seat blocks on the header beam and moon beam generally have high douqi (block slope), accounting for 5/9 of the block height, while Song dynasty douqi only accounted for 2/5 of the block height. Due to its special proportion (tentatively called "high-leg block"), its function is similar to a short column (shuzhu) used to raise the tie beam.

Generally, eave columns have a simple one-tier dougong, called "doukotiao" in "Yingzao Fashi" (Figure 11-5): the ludou extends a nidao gong horizontally to support the column header tie beam and eave, and extends a huagong one tier longitudinally outward, with a linggong on the tier head, a timu (substitute wood) supporting the liaoyan (eave purlin), inwardly reducing gong to support the moon beam. The moon beam is sometimes connected with the shoutou (bracket arm tip) on the linggong and reinforced by intersecting with horizontal tie beams; the shoutou is made as maye cloud (hemp leaf cloud). In the late Qing and early Republican periods, some residences were greatly influenced by Jiangnan architecture, simply omitting dougong and cantilevering the xuan (ceiling) beam, making a decorative board (huaban) with the beam supporting the tie beam on top.

There is also a type of diagonal brace bracket (xicheng gong), with one end inserted into the column body or standing on a dingtou gong (T-head bracket), and the other end placing a dou to support the tie beam (photo 4-9). This diagonal brace bracket actually shares the same origin as the diagonal braces prevalent in Huizhou. Such diagonal braces in Huizhou and Dongyang became the focus of decoration; in the Ming dynasty, simpler patterns of flowing clouds and scrolling grass were still common, and by the Qing dynasty, elaborate round carvings appeared. This type of diagonal brace bracket in Wenzhou is very similar to such components in Yong'an and Taining areas of Fujian: the upper end holds a dou, the lower end is made as curved water pattern, with exquisite carving. Additionally, in Taishun and Pingyang areas, inserted bracket components similar to guandao gong (guan-knife bracket) can be seen, with some dougong degenerating into corolla shapes (Figure 11-3); this type of dougong is similar to practices in Longyan, Fujian and other places. The above two dougong practices both indicate mutual influence between Wenzhou and Fujian residences in woodworking.

3. Roof Surface

Wenzhou vernacular architecture overall looks very vivid and elegant. The creation of this charm is attributed on the one hand to various eaves, and on the other hand to roof treatment, using the techniques of juzhe (roof curvature), shengqi (ridge rise), and cejiao (column inclination). The vertical curvature of the roof is called juzhe, the horizontal curvature is called shengqi, and cejiao means columns incline toward the center.

Wenzhou's climate is hot and humid; houses need to avoid direct sunlight and also need to block wind, therefore the depth is large and eaves overhang deeply, making the roof surface very large. A large roof surface would be dull and monotonous; by using the three techniques of juzhe, shengqi, and cejiao, the house produces two curved surfaces. Looking at the house from the gable end, due to the juzhe technique, a slightly curved "人" (person) shape is produced (Figure 9-3); looking at the ridge from a height, due to the shengqi technique, a curve like a carrying pole slightly翘起 at both ends is produced (photos 1-5, 5-11), making the roof surface vivid and spiritual, and full of tension. Although the entire village is full of roofs, it is not oppressive, but instead has an亲和 and light atmosphere.

Here, even some single-slope roofs, and even the roofs of gatehouses and toilets, are treated with juzhe and shengqi. Its main method relies on "shengtou mu" (rise-head wood) or tile shimming. In Wenzhou vernacular architecture,凡是 small-scale,形象-complete buildings such as pavilions, village gates, paifang, and courtyard gates, cejiao is essential. This practice, first, strengthens the overall sense of the image; second, makes the structure more stable; third, sets off the舒展 and elegance of the roof.

4. Small Woodwork (Xiaomuzuo)

In residences, lattice doors (geshan men) are often installed behind the front corridor; the door panel center generally has relatively simple lattice patterns (see photos 4-16, 4-18), mostly straight bars interlaced in palace-style or book-strip style, rarely using curved patterns, unlike the elaborate lattice patterns in Huizhou and southern Jiangsu. Ming-style willow-bar windows are also quite common, while eaves generally install straight-bar lattice windows. In short, mountain villagers in Wenzhou advocate simplicity and nature, disliking extravagance, so the entire finishing is also less ornate, with more of a simple scholarly air (photos 4-17, 4-20).

The woodworking system of Wenzhou residences is less standardized and purer than official-style woodworking, instead presenting more diversity — influenced by different regions and eras, mutually融合 and learning from each other, of course without losing local characteristics. For example, although the Wenzhou region was influenced by the woodworking of residences in Jiangsu, Anhui, Fujian, and within the province, it still preserves its own valuable woodworking tradition, namely the inherited Song dynasty legacy and the fashion of simplicity, nature, and love of natural curved timber. Therefore, in the study of residential woodworking, one must not only sort out the characteristics of its own woodworking, but also make vertical and horizontal connections: on the one hand, exploring the historical evolution of woodworking; on the other hand, examining the mutual influence of folk woodworking in various regions. Another important clue is the mutual connection between official-style architecture and folk architecture. The two are not "井水不犯河水" (mutually non-interfering), but mutually exchange and learn from each other. This is just like cultural arts such as dance and opera: folk culture is the source and foundation of official art or high art, providing nourishment for it, while official art in turn influences folk creation.

chapters.name: 第三章 温州乡土建筑的传统精神

sections.name: 一、门—院—屋三段式的居住模式
sections.content_zh:
一、门—院—屋三段式的居住模式

温州位于中华文化圈内，其民居无疑要受传统文化的影响而具有一定的传统精神，但是这种传统是特定环境下的传统，与浙北、皖南等地民居比较，又有自己的特色。

多去乡间走走，不难发现，我国古代乡土民居基本上由门—院—屋三部分组成。门是入口，有疆界和防卫意义；院一般作为晒场、果园、堆放杂物、放养家畜等用；屋住人。院的布局形式，有前院、后院、侧院，大户人家，由屋的排列方式不同形成了三合院、四合院、日月形的院，以及众多的内院。这些内院，如果面积不大的话就叫做"天井"。

温州乡土民居的门—院—屋三段式的精神也是很强烈的（照6-1～照6-9）。平阳顺溪陈氏四份即老四古宅，有四个大院子，六个天井；永嘉芙蓉大型民居——司马弟（图7-1）由三座四合院并组成一幢大房子，进门后是三个院子，还有两个花园，右侧面也有一个大院，左侧有窄长小院，里面还有三个内院。泰顺雪溪胡宅（石门楼）有六个内院，四个外院（照14-3）。泰顺三魁下武洋林家厝有内院九个，外院六个（图9-1）。小户人家的院落不那么规则，但院落是一定有的（照6-6，照6-7）。用地紧张的农户，宁可砍掉房屋一角，也要设个小院（照6-8，照6-9）。院除了有实用功能外，还有纳天地于家的精神功能，由于有了这个见"天"的空间，住屋本身反而退居到次要的地位了。
sections.content_en:
1. Gate-Courtyard-House Three-Stage Residential Model

Wenzhou is located within the Chinese cultural sphere, and its vernacular residences undoubtedly have a certain traditional spirit influenced by traditional culture. However, this tradition is a tradition under specific circumstances, and compared with residences in northern Zhejiang and southern Anhui, it has its own characteristics.

Walking more in the countryside, it is not difficult to find that ancient Chinese vernacular residences basically consist of three parts: gate-courtyard-house. The gate is the entrance, with boundary and defense significance; the courtyard generally serves as a drying ground, orchard, storage for杂物, and livestock raising; the house is for living. The layout forms of courtyards include front courtyards, back courtyards, and side courtyards. For large families, different arrangements of houses form three-sided courtyards, quadrangles, sun-moon shaped courtyards, and numerous inner courtyards. These inner courtyards, if not large in area, are called "tianjing" (sky wells).

The gate-courtyard-house three-stage spirit of Wenzhou vernacular residences is also very strong (photos 6-1 to 6-9). The Chen family's fourth branch (old four) ancient residence in Shunxi, Pingyang, has four large courtyards and six sky wells. The large residence in Furong, Yongjia — Sima Di (Figure 7-1) — consists of three quadrangles combined into one large house, with three courtyards after entering the gate, two gardens, a large courtyard on the right side, a narrow and long courtyard on the left, and three inner courtyards inside. The Hu residence (Shimenlou) in Xuexi, Taishun, has six inner courtyards and four outer courtyards (photo 14-3). The Lin family residence in Xiawuyang, Sankui, Taishun, has nine inner courtyards and six outer courtyards (Figure 9-1). Small households' courtyards are less regular, but courtyards are definitely present (photos 6-6, 6-7). Farmers with tight land would rather cut off a corner of the house than fail to set up a small courtyard (photos 6-8, 6-9). Besides practical functions, the courtyard also has the spiritual function of bringing heaven and earth into the home; because of this space that sees the "sky," the residence itself反而 recedes to a secondary position.

key_terms.en: Chen family ancient residence, Shunxi, Pingyang

sections.name: 二、臻于表礼的入口
sections.content_zh:
二、臻于表礼的入口

"道"与"器"在中国古代有很重要的对应概念。建筑是"器"，但是中国是礼义之国，建筑这个"器"必定要带上道德符号。门通常有两个特征：一是有很强的表礼特征，黄帝宅经说"宅以门户为冠带，门是主人身份的表征，因此，都将门、屋同等对待，有的以"屋门"形式出现，门上做脊、翘角、檐和装饰性斗栱，是屋的形象的缩写和提示（照7-2，照7-4）。"墙门"形式的门普遍做法是门向里退缩，形成一个"八"字型空间（照7-3）。江南一带把"命好"叫做"八字好"，大概这就是"八"字形门的风水学意义吧。"八"字门又不禁使人们联想起京剧中"大人物"出场时的程式化台步——"八"字步，两者的文化内涵是相同的。

我们的祖先又是十分善于处理"情"与"理"的关系的，他们总是把器做得"合情合理"，在满足礼的前提下，贯注着对美的追求。有些人家的入口处理，比较注重自然，讲究实惠，有的门除了有风水学所讲的"纳气就势"的意义外，还巧妙地解决了房屋临街（路）用地局促的矛盾（照7-6），创造出一个"入口前空间"，弹丸之地见功夫（照7-5）。有的不直接向家园开口，而是曲折过渡一下，提升了家庭气氛的私密感（照7-7，照7-8）。
sections.content_en:
2. Entrance Reaching Ritual Expression

"Dao" (way) and "qi" (vessel) had very important corresponding concepts in ancient China. Architecture is "qi" (vessel), but China is a nation of ritual and righteousness, so architecture as a "vessel" must carry moral symbols. Gates usually have two characteristics: first, they have strong ritual expression features. The Yellow Emperor's House Classic says "a house takes its gate as its crown and belt; the gate is a表征 of the owner's status." Therefore, gates and houses are treated equally; some appear in the form of "house gates," with ridges, upturned corners, eaves, and decorative dougong on the gate, serving as an abbreviation and提示 of the house's image (photos 7-2, 7-4). The common practice of "wall gate" form is that the gate recedes inward, forming a "八" (eight)-shaped space (photo 7-3). In the Jiangnan region, "good fortune" is called "good eight-character," which is probably the feng shui meaning of the "八"-shaped gate. The "八"-shaped gate also inevitably reminds people of the stylized stage steps of "important figures" in Peking opera — the "八"-character steps; the cultural connotations of both are the same.

Our ancestors were also very good at handling the relationship between "qing" (emotion) and "li" (reason). They always made vessels "reasonable and appropriate," infusing the pursuit of beauty under the premise of satisfying ritual. Some families' entrance treatment emphasizes nature and practicality; some gates, besides the feng shui meaning of "receiving qi and following the form," also cleverly solve the contradiction of tight land for houses facing streets (roads) (photo 7-6), creating an "entrance front space" where even a tiny space shows skill (photo 7-5). Some do not open directly to the home, but make a winding transition, enhancing the privacy of the family atmosphere (photos 7-7, 7-8).

key_terms.en: Receiving qi and following form (feng shui)

sections.name: 三、藏的文化心理图式与围的空间处理手法
sections.content_zh:
三、"藏"的文化心理图式，"围"的空间处理手法

温州人的投资方向，有一种"走归"的心理定势。人们在外面当官、经商发财了，总是要把财产投放到家乡，以买田置宅为上，这本身就是"藏"的文化心理图式的表现。在处理我与他，内与外的关系和建筑艺术造型上，更加体现"藏"的原则。有些房屋内部气势恢宏，但外表朴素无华，"英华积于中"，"和顺形乎外"，将强大的力量藏在朴素、稳定、和谐的外表之中，将小天地藏在家里（照8-1）。如泰顺雪溪清朝贡生胡辛伟家，内部气势磅礴，外表却一副农家样子，连表礼特征最强的门台也用普通的村屋遮去（照8-2）。"藏"，还表现在住宅选址的环境意识里：人们喜欢把家园建在有依靠的大背景里（参照1-10），为了争取交通便利和阴凉，巧妙地顺着河滩，围绕桥头，靠着大树、山脚营舍筑屋。哪怕是悬岩下，山腰上，也能像树一样建上几幢房子。那些散落在溪谷之间、篁竹之中的村落，轮廓线错落有致，如山，建筑风格朴素凝练，如水，流露出来的气韵闲远冲淡，如云，可用"屋宇同位"，"三理（天理、地理、生理）合一"八个字来概括这些房子的底蕴（参照1-3）。

温州民居的平面布局也隐现着"藏"的底蕴。大户人家的平面多呈封闭型，如"口"、"日"、"目"、"皿"、"田"等类型，由房屋本身围合成许多封闭空间。那些开口型的房屋，也总是要用厚墙将家院"藏"起来。外墙面上很少开门，利用天井、院落把头上的青天、远处的山峰借过来，"藏"在家中（照8-4）。为了换得建筑构图上、心理上的私密和安全感，故意将入口退、折布置，甚至连门口也用影壁遮去外人的视线，达到藏室于内、藏情于里的目的（照8-7）。

"藏"的文化心理图式，又衍生出建筑的恋土品格和内聚性质，以及"俭"、"朴"、"团"、"蓄"的治家模式。如平阳顺溪陈氏古宅，采用院落相套、纵深发展的形式一代一代、一进一进贴着地面发展，总建筑面积达4200m²，有六个天井、四个院子、99个间套房，宁可失去一些采光条件和耕地面积，也不向上升腾发展，将庞大的建筑群收聚在生他养他的土地上。苍南金乡镇沈宅，朴素端庄的大门台内藏有六个小门台、六个院落，尤其是该宅的入口部分，藏了一个富有哲意的小宇宙。反宇屋顶，两头外放，中间内倾，神态张扬，强化了结构的内聚性质。至于要"飞"出去的飞檐翘角，最后还是收回来，将它的张力感收聚在地心。

"聚族而居"也有"藏"的原型心里在起作用。积家为族，聚族成村，村村有族长、村规，族人讲求团结、崇拜集体，甚至于发展到党团乡里、山头宗派等，都是"藏"的文化心理的正质和负质。为了把时间意识的藏转化成空间的藏，姓姓写族谱、建宗祠，村村筑寨墙、砌寨门。于是，严肃的宗祠、粗犷的寨墙里"藏"着世代相传的宗族意识，崇山峻岭中藏着"封闭"、"真"、"犷"的古村落（参照1-7）。
sections.content_en:
3. "Concealment" Cultural Psychological Schema and "Enclosure" Spatial Processing Technique

Wenzhou people's investment direction has a psychological set of "returning home." When people become officials or prosper in business outside, they always invest their property in their hometown, prioritizing buying land and houses — this itself is a manifestation of the "concealment" cultural psychological schema. In handling the relationship between self and other, interior and exterior, and in architectural artistic modeling, the principle of "concealment" is even more embodied. Some houses have a magnificent interior but a plain and unadorned exterior, with "essence accumulated within" and "harmony manifested without," concealing powerful strength within a plain, stable, and harmonious exterior, hiding a small world within the home (photo 8-1). For example, the home of Hu Xinwei, a Qing dynasty tribute student in Xuexi, Taishun, has a磅礴 interior but a farmhouse-like exterior; even the gate platform with the strongest ritual features is concealed by an ordinary village house (photo 8-2). "Concealment" is also manifested in the environmental awareness of residence site selection: people like to build their homes in a large background with support (see reference 1-10); to gain transportation convenience and shade, they cleverly follow river beaches, surround bridgeheads, and build houses against large trees and mountain foothills. Even under overhanging rocks or on mountainsides, several houses can be built like trees. Those villages scattered among valleys and bamboo groves have错落有致 outlines, like mountains; the architectural style is simple and concise, like water; the revealed charm is leisurely and distant, like clouds. The essence of these houses can be summarized by the eight characters "house and environment co-located" and "three principles (heavenly principle, geographical principle, physiological principle) unified" (see reference 1-3).

The plane layout of Wenzhou residences also reveals the connotation of "concealment." Large families' planes are mostly enclosed, such as "口" (mouth), "日" (sun), "目" (eye), "皿" (vessel), "田" (field) types, with the houses themselves enclosing many closed spaces. Those open-type houses always use thick walls to "conceal" the home courtyard. Doors are rarely opened on exterior walls; using sky wells and courtyards, the blue sky above and distant mountain peaks are borrowed and "concealed" within the home (photo 8-4). To gain privacy and security in architectural composition and psychology, the entrance is deliberately recessed and folded, and even the doorway uses a screen wall to block outsiders'视线, achieving the purpose of concealing rooms within and emotions within (photo 8-7).

The "concealment" cultural psychological schema also衍生出 the earth-loving character and inward-gathering nature of architecture, as well as the family management modes of "thrift," "simplicity," "unity," and "accumulation." For example, the Chen family ancient residence in Shunxi, Pingyang, adopts the form of nested courtyards and depth development, developing generation by generation, hall by hall close to the ground, with a total building area of 4200m², six sky wells, four courtyards, and 99 suites. Rather than lose some lighting conditions and arable land area, it does not develop upward, gathering the庞大 building complex on the land that gave birth to and raised it. The Shen residence in Jinxiang Town, Cangnan, has six small gate platforms and six courtyards concealed within the simple and dignified main gate platform; especially the entrance part of this residence conceals a philosophical small universe. The upturned-eave roof, with both ends outward and the middle inward, has an expressive demeanor, strengthening the inward-gathering nature of the structure. As for the flying eaves and upturned corners that want to "fly" out, they ultimately retract, gathering their sense of tension toward the earth's center.

"Living in clan groups" also has the prototype psychology of "concealment" at work. Accumulating families into clans, gathering clans into villages, every village has a clan chief and village rules; clan members emphasize unity and worship the collective, even developing into village factions and mountain sectarianism — all are positive and negative qualities of the "concealment" cultural psychology. To transform the concealment of time consciousness into spatial concealment, every surname writes genealogy and builds ancestral halls, every village builds village walls and village gates. Thus, solemn ancestral halls and rough village walls "conceal" the clan consciousness passed down through generations, and high mountains and steep ridges conceal "closed," "authentic," and "rugged" ancient villages (see reference 1-7).

key_terms.term: 英华积于中和顺形乎外
key_terms.en: Essence accumulated within, harmony manifested without
Chen family ancient residence, Shunxi, Pingyang (4200sqm)

sections.name: 四、生动玲珑的屋顶
sections.content_zh:
四、生动、玲珑的屋顶

高台基、木构架、大屋顶是中国古建筑的三大特色。我国古建筑学家林徽因女士说："在外形上，三者之中，最庄严美丽、迥然殊异于他系建筑，为中国建筑博得最大荣誉的，自是屋顶部分"（梁思成《清式营造则例》）。

中国传统建筑的大屋顶思想，表现在温州乡土的那些宗祠、书院、庙宇、亭子的大屋顶自不必说，在过去朝中命官巨贾的乡土大住宅中，就得到充分体现。这些人在故乡造的居屋，体量很大，当地人称之为"大屋"。当你步入建有这些"大屋"的乡村，扑入眼帘的是一片瓦浪，隐没在绿树中的掌着张力的屋脊和生动的飞檐翘角，玲珑古朴，气势张扬，加上屋脊上的龙蛇鸟兽等装饰及古朴的瓦当，瓦当上各色各样的植物纹、几何纹、雷纹、人形纹等，令人心旷神怡，它不禁使人们想起《阳宅集成》中的两句诗："万瓦鳞鳞井市中，高连屋脊是来龙……"，这就是古代中国以"龙"自称的缘由（照9-1～照9-5）。即使是一般民居，也是极重视屋顶，房屋的平面很简单，重点就在屋面上发展。不过，农家因受实用品格的支配，它的屋顶文化孕化为前面已说的"檐"文化精神。
sections.content_en:
4. Vivid and Exquisite Roofs

High platform bases, timber frames, and large roofs are the three major characteristics of ancient Chinese architecture. Ms. Lin Huiyin, a Chinese ancient architecture scholar, said: "In terms of exterior form, among the three, the most solemn and beautiful, distinctly different from other architectural systems, and winning the greatest honor for Chinese architecture, is naturally the roof part" (Liang Sicheng, "Qing-style Building Rules").

The large roof concept of traditional Chinese architecture is expressed in the large roofs of Wenzhou's vernacular ancestral halls, academies, temples, and pavilions — needless to say, it is fully embodied in the large vernacular residences of former court officials and wealthy merchants. These houses built in their hometowns have large volumes, called "big houses" by locals. When you step into a village with these "big houses," what meets your eyes is a sea of tile waves; the tension-bearing ridges and vivid flying eaves and upturned corners hidden among green trees are exquisite, simple, and imposing. Coupled with decorations of dragons, snakes, birds, and beasts on the ridges and simple tile ends (wadang), with various plant patterns, geometric patterns, thunder patterns, and human figure patterns on the tile ends, it is refreshing and delightful. It inevitably reminds people of two lines of poetry from "Yangzhai Jicheng" (Integrated Residences): "Ten thousand tiles scale-like in the market, high connecting ridges are the coming dragon..." — this is the reason ancient China called itself "dragon" (photos 9-1 to 9-5). Even ordinary residences attach great importance to roofs; the house plane is very simple, with the focus on developing the roof surface. However, due to the practical character of farmers, their roof culture gestated into the "eave" cultural spirit mentioned earlier.

key_terms.en: High platform, timber frame, large roof (three features)
Yangzhai Jicheng (Integrated Residences, feng shui text)

sections.name: 五、肇于实用进乎自然的理水文化
sections.content_zh:
五、肇于实用，进乎自然的理水文化

水是人类生命之源，人类从水中走出来以后，它作为人类的主要生产、生活、精神要素伴随左右，人们在居住文化中确立了"枕山、环水、面屏"的居住模式，形成镇环四流，因水成街，因水成村的景观。

我国居住文化中的理水活动，走过了一条肇于实用，进乎自然，深于精神的道路。

温州乡土建筑中的理水精神是非常强烈的，水，主要是作为一种自然环境和实用精神进入居住文化。如照10-1～照10-4所示，永嘉岩头浚水街，一渠清水，穿镇而过，它是居民洗涤之源，生活之链，既能增强人们的秩序观念、群体意识，同时又起了审美意义上的以空间换时间，集小景为大景的作用。芙蓉村的芙蓉池（参照10-5）及苍坡村的仁济庙（照11-9），是村民的公共休憩活动场所，它不仅有实用和审美意义，还有风水学上的深层意义，它有提醒村民的环境意识，重温文化空间，使族风村俗世代相传作用。至于大量的依山傍水的建筑家园中的水，除实用意义外，还起家庭空间背景的基座作用，如照10-7屋主人巧妙地设置了门屋这个过渡空间，实现了家庭与水的对话。至于某些官宦儒士家庭的理水之水（参照7-19），则是作为人的思辨对象，内心体验进入的。
sections.content_en:
5. Water Management Culture: Originating from Practicality, Advancing toward Nature

Water is the source of human life. After humans emerged from water, it has accompanied them as a major element of production, life, and spirit. In residential culture, people established the residential model of "pillowing mountains, encircling water, facing a screen," forming landscapes where towns are surrounded by flowing water, streets are formed because of water, and villages are formed because of water.

Water management activities in Chinese residential culture have followed a path: originating from practicality, advancing toward nature, and deepening into spirit.

The water management spirit in Wenzhou vernacular architecture is very strong. Water mainly enters residential culture as a natural environment and practical spirit. As shown in photos 10-1 to 10-4, the water street in Yantou, Yongjia, has a clear channel of water passing through the town. It is the source of washing for residents and a chain of life; it can enhance people's sense of order and group consciousness, while also playing an aesthetic role of exchanging space for time and gathering small scenes into a large scene. The Furong Pool in Furong Village (see reference 10-5) and the Renji Temple in Cangpo Village (photo 11-9) are public rest and activity places for villagers. They not only have practical and aesthetic significance, but also have deep feng shui significance: they remind villagers of environmental awareness, revisit cultural spaces, and pass down clan customs and village traditions through generations. As for the water in the numerous homes built against mountains and beside waters, besides practical significance, it also serves as the base of the family space background. For example, in photo 10-7, the homeowner cleverly set up the gatehouse as a transition space, realizing a dialogue between the family and water. As for the water management in certain official and scholar families (see reference 7-19), it enters as an object of human contemplation and inner experience.

key_terms.en: Pillowing mountains, encircling water, facing a screen
Streets and villages formed because of water

chapters.name: 第四章 温州乡土建筑中的公共建筑

sections.name: 一、宗祠
sections.content_zh:
一、宗祠

温州境内丘陵起伏，河流众多，山体被河流割切得支离破碎，常构成奇异的山峰和封闭的谷口、盆地。居住在这些闭塞环境里的人们，宗族意识较之平原的人更强，反映在居住形态上，积家成族，聚族成村，一村一姓或几个姓的现象特别明显。宗族社会的公共建筑，也就特别多，如各式各样的宗祠、亭、书院等，起到了村落风貌的结构性作用。

由于村寨防护（包括心理安全感）上的需要，寨寨都造寨墙，建寨门（照1-3，照1-7）。为了维系宗族成员的思想，每个氏族都写族谱，建宗祠。为了族人的歇息、交会还普遍造亭子等。

宗法社会里的人，荣宗耀祖、竖碑立传思想极浓。科举成名、当官、发财的人，都要在家乡求田问舍，铺路建亭。反之，乡亲们也都积极为这些人造牌坊，建纪念亭等。古代由于族权和政权合在一起，所以，从国家到百姓的观念中都是把公共建筑放在首位。《礼记·曲礼》曰："宗庙为先，厩库为次，居室为后"，这一现象，可称为"古代村落的教化建筑优先"原则。本文所提供的大量宗祠牌坊，就是这个文化背景下的产物。

在我国农村中常可看到的宗族祠堂（有的地方叫××氏大厅），在唐汉以前是没有的，宗祠的前身是家庙或称祠堂，秦朝时，只有豪族大户的墓地里建有类似于帝王陵寝的建筑。民间祠堂起源于西汉，是家族、宗族追念祭礼祖先的建筑物，"汉世多建祠堂于墓所"，后来逐渐移建于村落之中。唐朝，只允许品官、士族建立。宗祠的兴起、推广得力于宋代理学家朱熹、陆九渊等人的倡导，他们从稳定社会的角度提出建祠。朱熹在《家礼》中极力宣扬农村设祠的重要性，宣扬以此举"报本反始之心，尊祖敬宗之意，实有名分之守，所以开业传世之本。"但是这种祠堂也还是附于居室的，独立于居室之外的宗祠，是明代中叶以后的事。

《中国居住文化》（丁俊清．上海：同济大学出版社，1997年版）一书中讲到，聚族而居是我国居住文化的一大特点。我国历史上，人口举族迁移始于晋，南宋以后开始大规模迁移。作者查阅过很多家谱、地名志，温州很多名门望族都是这个时期从各地（主要是北方）迁移而来，清初的海禁运动，又从南方迁移来不少氏族。他们或单独立村，或与土著结合，通过联姻和地缘关系形成具有典型江南色彩的一种宗族形态，反映在村落形态上则是出现众多的单姓、复姓村落。宗族的社会功能是多方面的，但主要表现在对以自然村落为基本居住形态的农村社会生活的有效组织和协调上。根据古代学者班固对"宗族"内涵进行的阐发，"宗族"具有"纪理"和"会聚"族内成员两方面的意义，他说："宗，尊也，为先祖主也……所以长和睦也。大宗能率小宗，小宗能率弟，通其有无，所以纪理族人者也，""族者溱也，聚也。谓思复相依溱也，上溱高祖下至玄孙，一家有吉，百家聚之，合而为亲，生相亲复，死相哀痛，有会聚之道，故谓之族。"（班固，白虎通卷8）

综上，温州农村有这么一个社会背景，宗族又有这么两个主要职能，反映在建筑活动上，是大兴宗祠建设。宗祠的分布，先是一姓一祠，时间长了，人口多了，就发展成一宗一祠。

我国古代村落宗祠，本身是个礼制建筑，同时又受礼制的约束，它的发展历程，是由墓庙到家庙，纪念故人的代数也有规定，明初还是沿用朱熹《家礼》旧制，人可祭祖父母、父母；洪武十七后（公元1384年）改民祭礼两代为曾、祖、祢"三代，后又发展为"高、曾、祖、祢"四代，到清代打破了这一规定，而是向上延伸至几十世。由于世代的延续，人口的增多，村落中先是一姓一祠就变成一宗一祠，于是出现了"大宗祠"（照11-1）、"小宗祠"（照11-3）。

作为礼制建筑，宗祠的型制和外形比较保守、定型和封闭。

关于祠堂建筑的具体要求，《鲁班经》卷一说："凡造祠宇为之家庙，前三门，次东西走马廊，又次之大所，此之后明楼，茶亭，亭之后即寝堂。若装修自三门做起至内堂止。中门开四尺六寸二分，阔一丈三尺三分，……两边耳门三尺六寸四分，阔九尺七寸，……中门两边俱后格式。家庙不比寻常，人家子弟贤否能在此处钟秀，又且寝堂及听雨廊至三门只可步步高，儿孙方有尊卑……"温州的宗祠或支祠，大都遵循此制，但各祠又因宗族经济状况的不同而在型制上与装修上又有所差别。

祠多为三开间，两进或三进；分门屋，享堂，寝堂，东西庑。每两进中间为天井。祠堂内主要大厅都在第二进，称为享堂（照11-4），其进深较其他各进都大，梁架也高大华丽。金柱间多为五架。寝堂进深往往最小（照11-2，照11-4，11-6）。

宗祠每往里一进，地平就或多或少地抬高，到寝堂时达到最高，这种空间处理方式有着建筑本身以外的特别含义，在《鲁班经》中已有明确的记述。

门屋、享堂、寝堂和两庑的前檐全部开敞，室内空间与院落融成一体。从门屋向上可一直望到寝堂，三重室内空间和两进院落，在正午阳光的照耀之下形成极富韵律的明暗对比。宗族香火的延续仿佛在这深邃而又富有明暗变化的空间里得以实现。

宗祠是农村宗族社会里品位最高的公共建筑，它表征着宗族或宗族下房的经济、社会和政治地位，是团结整个宗族、维系人伦秩序、炫耀乡邻、提高族人自尊的载体。永嘉塘湾村郑氏大宗祠里的一副楹联："萃子孙于一堂，序照序穆；享祖宗以万檀，报德报功，"概括了宗祠的这一作用。

宗祠的主要作用是供奉祖宗，按时举行祭礼，并且在此举行大会，议事，定期展示祭器、祖先画像、族谱，修谱也是在宗祠里进行的。有些地方，宗祠还作为村族的临时公廨，地方官吏来，就在此歇宿。农忙时，宗祠则有生产性建筑的意义，它可堆稻谷、存杂物及族人的公共财物。每逢过年过节，宗祠极大地发挥寓教化于娱乐的作用，人们在里面跳绳、踢毽子、玩铜线游戏及至摆酒席、赌博。最牵动人心的是演戏，每遇于此，早几天就带口信或亲自出村邀请亲戚朋友来赶热闹。温州是南戏的故乡，小曲、谣辞、艳史等不入雅座的俗文化十分发达，村宗祠里的戏台（照11-1，照11-3），是这种文化的温床。宗祠的轴心整合、教化作用是不言而喻的，永嘉《珍川朱氏族谱》中写道："为子孙者，睹规制之伟宏，则思祖德之宽远；见栋宇之巍焕，则思祖业之崇深"。泰顺三魁镇庵前村张氏宗祠有一幅楹联写道："祠依东山后裔昌盛，堂迎武水世代长流"。泰顺筱村吴氏宗祠（照11-5）有一楹联为："五溪水秀史册辉映四进士，凤林峰丽乔木丛生十名官"。甚至连宗祠的命名都有教化作用，如思远堂、孝思堂、敦睦堂、崇本堂、明德堂等，使人看到它，就"上体父祖培植之勤，下笃子孙忠缅之念，将书香振起"。

宗祠内装饰浑厚细腻，柱础多为石圆雕（参照5-12，照5-13，照5-14，照5-15），图案多为吉祥物，样式很多。如果宗族中有人做过大官，则柱础可用虎爪纹式样（参照5-17），与上面柱的断面形式配合默契。

经济实力强的宗祠或支祠都设有戏台（照11-1，11-3），位于第一进门屋的明间隔院与享堂相对。戏台向院子内凸出，结构与门屋脱离，而空间则是连续的，其面积约同于明间。戏台以门厅和两侧次间为后台，次间和梢间上部常做夹层，以扩大后台。戏台的三面完全向观众敞开。演戏时，天井及享堂的前檐下为男子观戏场所，享堂的前檐柱之后为妇女观戏场所。两部分之间临时可用矮栏杆隔开。

戏台台面高约1.5m（图2-3），沿台面边缘有大约30cm高的小栏杆。背靠门厅的一侧是太师壁，右边是名为"出将"的上场门，左边是名为"入相"的下场门。太师壁后有1m多宽的候场台，通门厅和夹层的小楼梯在这里上下。台面左侧有一个不大的副台，是伴奏乐队用的"场面"，有独立的扶梯。戏台位于中轴线上，紧挨门厅，为的是演戏敬祖，让祖宗能欣赏演出。但戏台却因此堵塞了中轴线上的交通，每逢举行重要的仪式时，有些舆轿和圣物必须从正门沿中轴线上进入正厅。所以，戏台面的台板通常不是整块的，沿中轴线有一排活动台板，可以抽掉，让路给舆轿。因此，宗祠正面必有三个门，中间的门一般不开而从两个梢间的门出入，这在《鲁班经》中也有记述。凸出于院中的戏台上面覆歇山屋顶，檐口较高。戏台形体完整，翼角飞扬，在正厅和廊庑的檐口水平线衬托下，非常抢眼，成为院落的视觉中心。戏台上方的藻井十分华丽，是温州最精致的木作之一（照4-10）。永嘉莒江下村和泰顺筱村镇吴氏宗祠的戏台上，都是斗八藻井，由四面枋子上平身科斗拱后尾出两翘后抹角成八角，再斜上出三翘，近似镏金斗拱。这些斗拱都作装饰化变形，精雕细刻，流云卷草，婉转曲折。

在传统的宗法制度下的血缘村落里，宗祠的祭祀活动既频繁又隆重，而且每次参加的人也很多，在这种情况下，组织工作就显得非常重要。在各族的宗谱里，都有宗祠祭祀的方式和规格，以便于对每次进行的祭祀或别的活动预先进行规定，好让活动能圆满完成。
sections.content_en:
1. Ancestral Halls (Zongci)

Wenzhou's territory has rolling hills and numerous rivers, with mountains cut into fragmented pieces by rivers, often forming strange peaks and enclosed valley mouths and basins. People living in these enclosed environments have stronger clan consciousness than those in plains. Reflected in residential forms, families accumulate into clans, clans gather into villages, and the phenomenon of one village with one surname or several surnames is particularly evident. Public buildings of clan society are therefore particularly numerous, such as various ancestral halls, pavilions, and academies, playing a structural role in the village's appearance.

Due to the need for village defense (including psychological security), every village builds village walls and village gates (photos 1-3, 1-7). To maintain the ideology of clan members, every clan writes genealogy and builds ancestral halls. For clan members' rest and gathering, pavilions are also commonly built.

In patriarchal society, people had a strong desire to glorify ancestors and erect monuments. Those who succeeded in imperial examinations, became officials, or made fortunes all bought land and built houses in their hometowns, paving roads and building pavilions. Conversely, villagers actively built memorial archways and pavilions for these people. In ancient times, because clan power and political power were united, from the state to common people, public buildings were placed first in concept. "Book of Rites · Qu Li" says: "Ancestral temple first, stables and warehouses second, residences third" — this phenomenon can be called the principle of "educational architecture priority in ancient villages." The numerous ancestral halls and archways provided in this article are products of this cultural background.

Clan ancestral halls (called "×× shi dating" in some places) commonly seen in China's countryside did not exist before the Tang and Han dynasties. The predecessor of ancestral halls was the family temple or shrine; during the Qin dynasty, only wealthy and powerful families had buildings similar to imperial mausoleums in their cemeteries. Folk shrines originated in the Western Han dynasty as buildings for families and clans to remember and sacrifice to ancestors. "In Han times, shrines were mostly built at gravesites," later gradually moved into villages. In the Tang dynasty, only officials and aristocratic families were allowed to build them. The rise and spread of ancestral halls benefited from the advocacy of Song dynasty Neo-Confucians Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan, who proposed building shrines from the perspective of social stability. In his "Family Rituals," Zhu Xi vigorously promoted the importance of setting up shrines in rural areas, advocating that this practice "expresses the heart of repaying origins and beginnings, the meaning of respecting ancestors and honoring clans, truly upholding status distinctions, and thus serving as the foundation for passing down the family business through generations." However, such shrines were still attached to residences; independent ancestral halls separate from residences only appeared after the mid-Ming dynasty.

The book "Chinese Residential Culture" (Ding Junqing. Shanghai: Tongji University Press, 1997 edition) states that living in clan groups is a major feature of Chinese residential culture. In Chinese history, clan migration began in the Jin dynasty, with large-scale migration starting after the Southern Song dynasty. The author has consulted many genealogies and place-name records; many prominent families in Wenzhou migrated from various places (mainly the north) during this period, and the sea ban movement in the early Qing dynasty brought many clans from the south. They either established villages independently or integrated with natives, forming a clan form with typical Jiangnan characteristics through marriage and geographical ties. Reflected in village forms, this resulted in numerous single-surname and multi-surname villages. The social functions of clans are multifaceted, but mainly manifested in the effective organization and coordination of rural social life with natural villages as the basic residential form. According to the ancient scholar Ban Gu's elaboration on the connotation of "clan," "clan" has two meanings: "managing" and "gathering" clan members. He said: "Zong (clan) means respect, being the master of ancestors... thus promoting harmony. The major clan can lead the minor clan, the minor clan can lead younger brothers, sharing what they have, thus managing clan members"; "Zu (clan) means gathering. It means mutual dependence, from great-great-grandfather down to great-great-grandson; when one family has good fortune, a hundred families gather, becoming relatives, loving each other in life and mourning each other in death, having the way of gathering, hence called clan." (Ban Gu, Baihu Tong, Volume 8)

In summary, Wenzhou's countryside has such a social background, and clans have these two main functions. Reflected in architectural activities, this means vigorously constructing ancestral halls. The distribution of ancestral halls began with one shrine per surname; over time, as population grew, it developed into one shrine per clan branch.

Ancient village ancestral halls in China were themselves ritual buildings,同时 constrained by ritual systems. Their development process went from tomb shrines to family temples, with regulations on the number of generations of ancestors commemorated. In the early Ming dynasty, Zhu Xi's "Family Rituals" old system was still followed, allowing people to sacrifice to grandparents and parents; after Hongwu 17 (1384 AD), the common people's sacrifice ritual was changed to two generations: great-grandfather, grandfather, and father ("three generations"), later developing into "great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father" four generations. By the Qing dynasty, this regulation was broken, extending upward to dozens of generations. Due to the continuation of generations and population growth, villages first had one shrine per surname, then became one shrine per clan branch, thus出现了 "major ancestral halls" (photo 11-1) and "minor ancestral halls" (photo 11-3).

As ritual buildings, the form and exterior of ancestral halls are relatively conservative,定型, and enclosed.

Regarding specific requirements for shrine architecture, "Lu Ban Jing" (Lu Ban Classic) Volume 1 says: "When building a shrine as a family temple, first the three gates, then the east and west horse-riding corridors, then the main hall, after that the clear tower, tea pavilion, and after the pavilion is the sleeping hall. If decorating, start from the three gates to the inner hall. The central gate opens four chi six cun two fen, width one zhang three chi three fen... the side gates three chi six cun four fen, width nine chi seven fen... both sides of the central gate follow the format. Family temples are unlike ordinary buildings; the worthiness of family's children can flourish here, and from the sleeping hall and listening-to-rain corridor to the three gates can only rise step by step, so that descendants have proper hierarchy..." Wenzhou's ancestral halls or branch shrines mostly follow this system, but each shrine differs in form and decoration due to different clan economic conditions.

Shrines are mostly three bays, with two or three halls; divided into gatehouse, worship hall, sleeping hall, and east-west side wings. Between each two halls is a courtyard (tianjing). The main hall in the shrine is always in the second hall, called the worship hall (photo 11-4), with greater depth than other halls, and tall and ornate beam frames. Between the golden columns is mostly five-frame. The sleeping hall's depth is often the smallest (photos 11-2, 11-4, 11-6).

Each time an ancestral hall goes inward one hall, the floor level is raised more or less, reaching the highest at the sleeping hall. This spatial treatment has special meaning beyond architecture itself, already clearly recorded in "Lu Ban Jing."

The front eaves of the gatehouse, worship hall, sleeping hall, and two side wings are all completely open, with indoor space merging with the courtyard. From the gatehouse one can see straight through to the sleeping hall; the three layers of indoor space and two courtyards, under the illumination of noon sunlight, form a rhythm-rich contrast of light and dark. The continuation of clan incense seems to be realized in this deep and light-dark-varying space.

Ancestral halls are the highest-status public buildings in rural clan society, representing the economic, social, and political status of a clan or its sub-branch. They are vehicles for uniting the entire clan, maintaining human ethical order, showing off to neighbors, and enhancing clan members' self-esteem. A couplet in the Zheng clan major ancestral hall in Tangwan Village, Yongjia reads: "Gathering descendants in one hall, ordering by seniority; offering ten thousand offerings to ancestors, repaying virtue and merit" — summarizing this function of ancestral halls.

The main function of ancestral halls is to enshrine ancestors, hold sacrifices at scheduled times, and hold assemblies and discussions here. Sacrificial vessels, ancestor portraits, and genealogies are regularly displayed, and genealogy revision is also conducted in ancestral halls. In some places, ancestral halls also serve as temporary public offices for the village clan; when local officials come, they rest here. During busy farming seasons, ancestral halls take on the meaning of productive buildings, storing rice grain,杂物, and clan public property. During festivals, ancestral halls greatly发挥 the role of integrating education into entertainment; people skip rope, kick shuttlecocks, play copper-wire games, and even set up banquets and gamble inside. The most touching is opera performances; whenever this happens, several days in advance people send messages or personally go out of the village to invite relatives and friends to join the excitement. Wenzhou is the hometown of Nanxi (southern drama), with highly developed popular culture such as ditties, ballads, and romantic tales not fitting elegant settings. The stages in village ancestral halls (photos 11-1, 11-3) are the breeding ground for this culture. The axial integration and educational function of ancestral halls is self-evident. The Yongjia "Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy" writes: "As descendants, seeing the grandeur of the regulations, one thinks of the breadth of ancestral virtue; seeing the magnificence of the building, one thinks of the depth of ancestral enterprise." The Zhang clan ancestral hall in Anqian Village, Sankui Town, Taishun has a couplet: "The shrine leans on the eastern mountain with descendants prosperous, the hall faces the martial water with generations flowing long." The Wu clan ancestral hall in Xiaocun, Taishun (photo 11-5) has a couplet: "Five streams' water shines with history reflecting four jinshi, Phoenix Peak's beauty with trees growing ten officials." Even the naming of ancestral halls has educational function, such as Siyuan Hall (Thinking of Origins), Xiaosi Hall (Filial Piety), Dunmu Hall (Harmony), Chongben Hall (Honoring Origins), Mingde Hall (Bright Virtue), etc., making people see it and "understand the diligence of ancestors' cultivation above, and deepen the thought of descendants' loyalty below, thus raising the scholarly tradition."

The interior decoration of ancestral halls is vigorous and delicate, with column bases mostly stone round carvings (see references 5-12, photos 5-13, 5-14, 5-15), with patterns mostly auspicious objects and many styles. If someone in the clan held a high official position, the column base can use tiger-claw pattern (see reference 5-17),配合默契 with the column cross-section form above.

Ancestral halls or branch shrines with strong economic power all have stages (photos 11-1, 11-3), located in the central bay of the first hall gatehouse, facing the worship hall across the courtyard. The stage protrudes into the courtyard, structurally separate from the gatehouse but spatially continuous, with area approximately equal to the central bay. The stage uses the gatehouse and two side bays as backstage, with the upper part of side bays and end bays often made into mezzanines to expand the backstage. The three sides of the stage are completely open to the audience. During performances, the courtyard and under the front eaves of the worship hall are for male audience, and behind the front eave columns of the worship hall are for female audience. The two parts can be temporarily separated by low railings.

The stage platform is about 1.5m high (Figure 2-3), with small railings about 30cm high along the platform edge. The side against the gatehouse is the taishi wall (master wall), the right side is the "Chujiang" (going out as general) entrance, and the left side is the "Ruxiang" (entering as minister) exit. Behind the taishi wall is a waiting platform over 1m wide, with small stairs to the gatehouse and mezzanine going up and down here. On the left side of the platform is a small副台, the "scene" for the accompanying band, with an independent ladder. The stage is located on the central axis, close to the gatehouse, for the purpose of performing opera to honor ancestors, allowing ancestors to enjoy the performance. However, the stage thus blocks traffic on the central axis; whenever important ceremonies are held, some sedan chairs and sacred objects must enter the main hall from the main gate along the central axis. Therefore, the stage platform boards are usually not a single piece; along the central axis there is a row of movable platform boards that can be removed to make way for sedan chairs. Thus, the front of the ancestral hall must have three doors, with the middle door generally not opened, and entry from the two end bay doors — this is also recorded in "Lu Ban Jing." The stage protruding into the courtyard is covered with a歇山 (hip-and-gable) roof, with high eaves. The stage form is complete, with wing corners flying, very eye-catching against the horizontal eave lines of the main hall and corridors, becoming the visual center of the courtyard. The caisson (zaojing) above the stage is very gorgeous, one of Wenzhou's most exquisite woodworks (photo 4-10). On the stages of the Wu clan ancestral halls in Lvjiangxia Village, Yongjia and Xiaocun Town, Taishun, there are douba caissons (octagonal caissons), formed by flat-set dougong on four sides' tie beams extending two arms then抹角 into octagons, then斜上出 three arms,近似 gilt dougong. These dougong are all decoratively transformed, exquisitely carved, with flowing clouds and scrolling grass, winding and graceful.

In traditional patriarchal blood-relation villages, the sacrificial activities of ancestral halls are both frequent and grand, with many participants each time. In this situation, organizational work becomes very important. In each clan's genealogy, there are methods and specifications for ancestral hall sacrifices, to pre-regulate each sacrifice or other activity, so that activities can be completed satisfactorily.

sections.content_zh:
二、亭

分布在温州各县的乡土公共建筑中，最富特征的是亭。亭的数量多（如永嘉县现存明、清时期的古亭就有300多个，泰顺县不少于500个），造型古朴浑厚，它的基本特点是具有宋风，与传统民居相映生辉。这些亭多数是村民捐资所建，未留下创作者姓名。千百年来，它们以其特殊的实用价值为村民提供了驻息场所，又以自身古朴清丽的风姿使绿水青山生韵，不断地激起后人的古国之思，由衷赞叹先民们强烈的社会责任感、朴实的感情以及那些"鬼斧神工"们不求闻达的创作精神（照12-15，照12-17）。

温州乡土建筑中的亭按其主要功能大致可分四种类型。

1. 路亭

这里的路亭，不是古代"长亭更短亭"送迎亲友的"望楼"，不是古代官府专为传递公文邮件在交通要道上设置的驿站，也不是给人家观赏的亭，它的主要功能是陶荫，供耕夫、旅人、樵民歇脚、坐息、饮茶、乘凉、避风雨。泰顺东溪仔亭有一幅对联："且停亭养养精神，请坐座谈谈国事"，可见亭还有教化作用。路亭选址大多位于山野路边，道路交叉口处，或山脚、泉水旁。亭与亭之间，有基本固定的距离。路亭大多为乡民自发集资兴建，也有不少是个人捐造的，他们不光是造亭，而且还要经营，供应凉茶和暑药等。如泰顺著名的罗阳石亭建于明正德十年（公元1515年），顶梁上刻着："温州府泰顺县知县郑典使真儒学训导喻东衡建造"，另两梁分别刻："仙居信士张宣捐资竖造"、"岭下信士林俊舍财经营"。1988年，原施主林、张氏的后裔对该亭进行了修葺。

有一种特殊的路亭，它不是造在路旁，而是跨路而造（照12-4），让道路穿亭而过，如泰顺三魁镇刘宅村古道桐山路建于清乾隆十五年（公元1750年）的石砌拱表隘门，当地人称"隘门亭"。泰顺有的村巷跨路建一个门楼，主要是驻憩用，也有标界、邻里意义。有的农村在村口的路旁，结合房屋建一"靠亭"。以上两类，可叫做"准亭"，这种不拘一格的做法，可见乡民们的社会责任感是多么强烈（照12-2，照12-3）。

路亭还有一个标界作用，建于县与县的交界处，如泰顺万排乡上排村，泰顺县与福鼎县交界处的分水亭，亭碑载："雍正七年（公元1729年）尼僧法章料鲁建。"

2. 村亭

这种亭可视作一村之"点睛"（照12-5），一般都建在村口（照12-7），也有位于村当中几条路的交叉口处（照12-8），或置于溪边，池塘上，主要供休息兼守卫、了望用，地方上也有人将之称为"凉亭"，是村人白天的主要公共活动空间（照12-9），尤其是老人，多在此度过晚年。凉亭还有一个分支，即位于田间地角的农亭。农人耕作疲惫或不胜烈日酷暑，便来亭小憩，抽烟饮茶，下雨时还可避雨，这种亭形体更为简单，流露出一派田园风味。不少村中建有露天戏台（照12-13）样子像亭，也是村民夏天乘凉的好地方，这种戏台也可认为是"准亭"。

3. 风水亭

由于风水思想的支配，村民多将亭与塔、树等同视，为保护风水的一种物质措施以求村庄的昌平，这类亭除有风水意义外，还有礼仪、议事的作用（照12-15，照12-16，照12-17）。

4. 纪念亭

如永嘉苍坡村的"望兄亭"、"送弟阁"，流传着一个美好的故事：相传宋建炎年间李氏兄弟分家，兄秋山主动迁居邻村方巷，兄弟情深，分居后往来甚密，分手后总要送至对方家门。后来兄弟俩商定各自在村口建一亭，隔溪相望，到家后马上在亭中悬灯以告归途平安。文成南田辞岭亭是为纪念刘基次子忠节公刘景进京而建（照12-19，照12-20）。

亭的平面布置讲究自然地形的利用，平面形状以正方形居多，另外有矩形、六角形、八角形、凸字形、T字形等。平面面积以十余平方米为多，内部空间多不分隔。在温州众多的古亭中，永嘉县水云村的赤水亭（照12-22）可算是亭中一奇了。该亭建于光绪十八年（公元1893年），平面呈"凸"字形，前为台，后为坛，基底面积达78m²。该亭因其建筑巧绝、亭中绘画美绝、题词文笔妙绝被当地人称之为"三绝亭"。永嘉县龙坎下村附近的路亭，巧妙地借用了地形的自然高差，将亭分为上下两级形成错层，紧靠路旁的下亭为路亭，通过台阶联系的上亭供村民休息纳凉、传播信息，上下两个空间独立又互相渗透，其空间组合之精巧令人赞叹不已。

这些亭经济实用，简单朴质，建筑式样往往是以农村中的实用建筑为蓝本，如民居、水车房、田间耕作的休息草棚。这里的亭体形虽简洁，但总缺不了塔柱间那圈"吴王靠"式坐椅，人们可在此坐下休息聊天，避雨乘凉，也可以横卧小睡，其他地方的亭大多没有如此装置，足见温州乡亭的实用意义。

亭由瓦顶、木构架、石台基组成。台基一般有柱角、板陡、条阶、台阶、地墁、柱础等，均用石材构成。但路亭、凉亭常以卵石、毛石构筑；风水亭、纪念亭则以条石、块石构筑。台基的高度一般为0.3～1.0m，风水亭的台基比较高，风格粗犷浑厚。

亭的承重结构为木构架，多为抬梁式。悬山顶做法简单，柱、梁、枋不经雕饰，为小式做法，挑檐桁直接架于梁上，歇山顶、五脊四坡和攒尖顶的木构架则稍为讲究些，用小式或大式木做，用料也粗。梁、柱或方或圆较规整，各式斗拱也讲究，还加各式柱饰。

亭的顶部做法主要有悬山顶、假歇山顶、攒角顶及五脊四坡顶、重檐歇山顶，最普遍的做法是歇山顶，风格和当地民居相同，流溢出浓郁的乡土气息。

亭的基本风格为宋风，虽然一些斗拱、雀接、榫头的做法带有明清民间装饰风格，但其主要的梁架结构以及形体比例都与明清时期的建筑不同，表现出较多的宋代木构遗风。

正方形歇山式亭，是温州地区最为普遍的一类亭。这类亭，平面基本是正方形，一般深阔各三间，金柱四根，檐柱12根，柱身有侧脚，檐下柱间设"吴王靠"。金柱较檐柱高，柱上皆施圆栌头，檐柱间以月梁形阑额联系，栌头上作"斗口跳"、泥道拱、两端承散斗，散斗上施替木或绰幕枋，再上承柱头枋，纵向栌斗外出华拱一跳，跳上交互斗上承替撩檐枋，纵向出耍头。内侧栌头减拱直接承明乳月，乳月的另一端插入金柱，这些都是比较典型的宋代《营造法式》的做法。转角处，柱身45°方向插丁头拱承托曲线形斜撑，撑上置斗承托相交的撩檐枋，内侧置45°明角乳，并伸出柱外承托老角梁。金柱之间做阑额。各间顶部皆施覆斗状天花。从立面上看举折较平缓，出檐深远，占柱高的一半，近似于宋代实例和《营造法式》规定。
sections.content_en:
2. Pavilions (Ting)

Among the vernacular public buildings distributed in various counties of Wenzhou, the most characteristic is the pavilion (ting). Pavilions are numerous (for example, Yongjia County has over 300 surviving ancient pavilions from the Ming and Qing dynasties, and Taishun County has no fewer than 500), with simple and vigorous forms. Their basic characteristic is Song dynasty style, shining alongside traditional residences. Most of these pavilions were built with donations from villagers, leaving no creator's name. For thousands of years, they have provided resting places for villagers with their special practical value, and with their simple and elegant forms have added charm to green mountains and clear waters, continuously inspiring later generations' thoughts of ancient times, sincerely praising the ancestors' strong sense of social responsibility, simple feelings, and the creative spirit of those "master craftsmen" who sought no fame (photos 12-15, 12-17).

Pavilions in Wenzhou vernacular architecture can be roughly divided into four types by their main functions.

1. Road Pavilions (Luting)

The road pavilions here are not the "wanglou" (watchtowers) of ancient "long pavilions and short pavilions" for seeing off and welcoming relatives and friends, nor the post stations specially set up by ancient government offices on major traffic routes for transmitting official documents and mail, nor pavilions for people to观赏. Their main function is to provide shade, for farmers, travelers, and woodcutters to rest, sit, drink tea, enjoy coolness, and shelter from wind and rain. The Dongxizai Pavilion in Taishun has a couplet: "Stop at the pavilion to nourish your spirit, please sit and discuss state affairs" — showing that pavilions also have educational functions. Road pavilions are mostly located by mountain roads, at road intersections, or at mountain foothills and beside springs. There is a basically fixed distance between pavilions. Road pavilions are mostly built with spontaneous fund-raising by villagers, and many are donated by individuals. They not only build pavilions but also manage them, supplying cool tea and summer medicine. For example, the famous Luoyang Stone Pavilion in Taishun was built in the 10th year of Ming Zhengde (1515 AD), with the top beam engraved: "Built by Zheng Dianshi, County Magistrate of Taishun, Wenzhou Prefecture, and Yu Dongheng, Confucianism Instructor"; the other two beams are respectively engraved: "Donated and erected by Zhang Xuan, a faithful scholar from Xianju" and "Financed and managed by Lin Jun, a faithful scholar from Lingxia." In 1988, descendants of the original donors Lin and Zhang renovated the pavilion.

There is a special type of road pavilion that is not built beside the road but across the road (photo 12-4), allowing the road to pass through the pavilion. For example, the stone arch gate at the ancient Tongshan Road in Liuzhai Village, Sankui Town, Taishun, built in the 15th year of Qing Qianlong (1750 AD), is locally called "Aimen Ting" (gate pavilion). Some villages in Taishun build a gatehouse across the lane, mainly for rest, also with boundary-marking and neighborhood significance. Some rural areas build a "leaning pavilion" beside the road at the village entrance, combined with houses. The above two types can be called "quasi-pavilions"; this不拘一格 approach shows how strong the villagers' sense of social responsibility is (photos 12-2, 12-3).

Road pavilions also have a boundary-marking function, built at county borders. For example, the Fenshui Pavilion at the border of Taishun County and Fuding County in Shangpai Village, Wanpai Township, Taishun, has a pavilion stele recording: "Built by Nun Fazhang in the 7th year of Yongzheng (1729 AD)."

2. Village Pavilions (Cunting)

This type of pavilion can be regarded as the "finishing touch" of a village (photo 12-5), generally built at the village entrance (photo 12-7), or at the intersection of several roads in the middle of the village (photo 12-8), or placed by streams and ponds. They mainly serve for rest, guard, and lookout; locals also call them "cool pavilions" (liangting), being the main public activity space for villagers during the day (photo 12-9), especially for the elderly, who often spend their later years here. Cool pavilions have a branch: farm pavilions located at field corners. When farmers are tired from plowing or overcome by the scorching sun, they come to the pavilion to rest, smoke and drink tea, and shelter from rain when it rains. This type of pavilion has a simpler form, revealing a pastoral flavor. Many villages have open-air stages (photo 12-13) that look like pavilions, also good places for villagers to enjoy coolness in summer; such stages can also be considered "quasi-pavilions."

3. Feng Shui Pavilions

Due to the支配 of feng shui thought, villagers often regard pavilions the same as pagodas and trees, as a material measure to protect feng shui and seek village peace and prosperity. Besides feng shui significance, this type of pavilion also has ritual and discussion functions (photos 12-15, 12-16, 12-17).

4. Memorial Pavilions

For example, the "Wangxiong Pavilion" (Looking at Brother Pavilion) and "Songdi Ge" (Seeing Off Brother Pavilion) in Cangpo Village, Yongjia, have a beautiful story: legend has it that during the Song Jianyan period, the Li brothers divided their family; the older brother Qiushan voluntarily moved to the neighboring Fangxiang Village. The brothers were deeply affectionate and visited frequently after separation, always escorting each other to the other's door after parting. Later the brothers agreed to each build a pavilion at the village entrance, facing each other across the stream, and upon arriving home immediately hang a lamp in the pavilion to inform of safe return. The Ciling Pavilion in Nantian, Wencheng, was built to commemorate Liu Jing, the loyal second son of Liu Ji, going to the capital (photos 12-19, 12-20).

The plane layout of pavilions emphasizes the use of natural terrain. Square shapes are most common, with others including rectangular, hexagonal, octagonal, convex-shaped, and T-shaped. Plane areas are mostly over ten square meters, with internal spaces mostly undivided. Among the many ancient pavilions in Wenzhou, the Chishui Pavilion in Shuiyun Village, Yongjia (photo 12-22) can be considered a wonder among pavilions. Built in the 18th year of Guangxu (1893 AD), its plane is "convex" shaped, with a platform in front and an altar behind, with a base area of 78m². The pavilion is called the "Three Wonders Pavilion" by locals for its exquisite architecture, beautiful paintings, and wonderful inscriptions. The road pavilion near Longkanxia Village, Yongjia, cleverly uses the natural height difference of the terrain, dividing the pavilion into upper and lower levels forming a split level. The lower pavilion close to the road is a road pavilion, while the upper pavilion connected by stairs serves for villagers' rest, cooling, and information dissemination. The upper and lower spaces are independent yet interpenetrating, with exquisite spatial combination that is amazing.

These pavilions are economical, practical, simple, and plain, with architectural forms often based on practical rural buildings, such as residences, watermill houses, and rest sheds for field farming. Although the pavilion forms here are simple, they always have the "Wu Wang Kao" (King Wu leaning) style chairs between columns, where people can sit and rest, chat, shelter from rain and enjoy coolness, or even lie down for a nap. Pavilions in other places mostly lack such installations,充分 showing the practical significance of Wenzhou village pavilions.

Pavilions consist of tile roofs, timber frames, and stone platform bases. The platform base generally has column corners, board slopes, steps, stairs, floor paving, and column bases, all made of stone. However, road pavilions and cool pavilions are often constructed with pebbles and rough stone; feng shui pavilions and memorial pavilions are constructed with dressed stone and block stone. The height of the platform base is generally 0.3-1.0m; feng shui pavilions have higher platform bases with a rough and vigorous style.

The load-bearing structure of pavilions is a timber frame, mostly post-and-lintel (tailiang) style. The overhanging gable (xuanshan) roof is simple in practice, with columns, beams, and tie beams not carved, in small-style practice, with overhanging eave purlins directly placed on beams. The timber frames of hip-and-gable (xieshan) roofs, five-ridge four-slope roofs, and pyramidal (zanjian) roofs are somewhat more elaborate, using small or large-style woodwork with粗 materials. Beams and columns, square or round, are relatively regular, with various dougong also elaborate, plus various column decorations.

The main roof practices of pavilions include overhanging gable, false hip-and-gable, pyramidal, five-ridge four-slope, and double-eave hip-and-gable. The most common practice is hip-and-gable, with the same style as local residences, exuding a strong rural atmosphere.

The basic style of pavilions is Song dynasty style. Although some dougong, sparrow braces, and tenon practices carry Ming-Qing folk decorative styles, their main beam frame structures and form proportions differ from Ming-Qing period buildings, showing more Song dynasty timber structure legacy.

Square hip-and-gable pavilions are the most common type in the Wenzhou area. These pavilions have a basically square plane, generally three bays in both depth and width, with four golden columns and 12 eave columns. Columns have cejiao (inclination), and "Wu Wang Kao" chairs are set between eave columns under the eaves. Golden columns are taller than eave columns, with round ludou (cap blocks) on top. Eave columns are connected by moon-beam-shaped lan'e (architrave), with "doukotiao" and nidao gong on the ludou, supporting sandou (intermediate blocks) at both ends, with timu (substitute wood) or chuomu fang on sandou, then supporting column header tie beams. Longitudinally, the ludou extends one tier of huagong, with jiaohudou on the tier head supporting the liaoyan fang (eave purlin), with shoutou (bracket arm tip) extending longitudinally. The inner ludou reduces gong to directly support the mingru yueliang (exposed moon beam), with the other end of the moon beam inserted into the golden column — these are all typical practices of the Song dynasty "Yingzao Fashi" (State Building Standards). At corners, dingtou gong (T-head brackets) are inserted at 45° from the column body to support curved diagonal braces, with dou on the braces supporting intersecting liaoyan fang. Inner 45° mingjiao ru (corner beam) is set, extending outside the column to support the old corner beam. Lan'e is made between golden columns. The top of each bay has an inverted-bucket-shaped ceiling. From the elevation, the juzhe (roof curvature) is relatively gentle, with deep eaves overhanging half the column height,近似 Song dynasty examples and "Yingzao Fashi" regulations.
